draft.title: Comparing insurance
card: Premium
the amount you pay to the insurer for the policy, often monthly or yearly. Yearly cost = monthly premium × 12.
Excess
the amount you pay first when you make a claim. The insurer pays the rest, up to the policy limit.
Cover
what the policy pays for. Read what is included and what is left out before you choose.

A lower premium often comes with a higher excess or less cover. To compare, check the cover is the same, then add the yearly premium and the excess for a claim year. Example: $50 a month with a $400 excess costs $600 + $400 = $1000 in a year with one claim.
draft.remember: Compare cover first, then the premium and excess together, not the premium alone.

a.q: Policy A costs $40 a month with a $500 excess. What is the total cost in a year with one claim?
a.why: Yearly premium = $40 × 12 = $480. Adding the $500 excess gives $980. $540 is wrong because it adds only one month of premium to the excess.
a.clue: Turn the monthly premium into a yearly amount first.

b.q: Both policies cover the same things. Policy X costs $35 a month with a $600 excess. Policy Y costs $45 a month with a $200 excess. Mia expects to make one claim this year. Which is cheaper, and by how much?
b.why: X costs $35 × 12 + $600 = $1020. Y costs $45 × 12 + $200 = $740. Y is cheaper by $280. X only looks cheaper if you compare premiums alone, and that gap is $120 a year.
b.clue: Find each policy's yearly premium, then add its excess.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers check out ($480 + $500 = $980, and $1020 − $740 = $280), and the card's example and explanations are correct.
